label: prop:regime-dependent-lower
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:regime-dependent-lower}
There exist universal constants $c,C>0$ such that the following holds.
Let $q\in(0,1]$, $R>0$, and $0<\mu\le\nicefrac{1}{3}$. Suppose that
\[
    n \ge
    \frac{C}{\mu^2} \cdot \max\Biggl\{
        \frac{1}{qR^2}\;\!,\;\!
        \exp\biggl(
            C \min\biggl\{
                \frac{R}{\sqrt{q}},\frac{1}{\mu}
            \biggr\}
            \log\biggl(\frac{e}{q}\biggr)
        \biggr)
    \Biggr\}.
\]
Then, the minimax risk satisfies
\[
    \mathfrak{R}_n(R,\mu,q)
    \ge
    \frac{c}{nq\mu^2} \cdot
    \begin{cases}
        \displaystyle
        \exp\left\{ c\frac{R}{\sqrt{q}}\right\},
        & \text{if } R\mu\le\sqrt{q},\\ 
        \displaystyle
        \exp\left\{
            \frac{c}{\mu} \log\left(1+\frac{1-q}{q}R^2\mu^2\right)
        \right\},
        & \text{if } \sqrt{q}<R\mu\le1,\\ 
        \displaystyle
        \exp\left\{\frac{c}{\mu}\log\left(\frac{1}{q}\right)\right\},
        & \text{if } R\mu>1.
    \end{cases}
\]

label: rem:proof-intuition
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:proof-intuition}
At this juncture, it is useful to pause to understand the intuition behind our construction through a heuristic calculation. 
For a complete observation $(Y,X)=(y,x(a,b))$, combining \crtCref{eq:generic-two-point-P1X} with the conditional laws of $Y$ under $P_0$ and $P_1$ yields
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}P_1}{\mathrm{d}P_0}(y,x(a,b))
=
e^{\alpha yb}F_\alpha(a,b)
=
e^{\alpha yb}\bigl\{\cosh(\alpha)-yb\sinh(\alpha) \cdot J(T)\bigr\}.
\]
If, heuristically, we could take $J(T)=1$, then
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}P_1}{\mathrm{d}P_0}(y,x(a,b))
=
e^{\alpha yb}\bigl\{\cosh(\alpha)-yb\sinh(\alpha)\bigr\}
=
e^{\alpha yb}e^{-\alpha yb}
=
1.
\]
Thus, the factor $F_\alpha$ is designed to cancel exactly the change in the conditional law of $Y$ induced by perturbing $\theta_0$ to $\theta_1$. Of course, an odd function $J$ cannot satisfy $J(T) \equiv c$ uniformly for any constant $c \neq 0$. Instead, we construct $J$ so that $\mathbb{E}_0[J(T)\mid T_S]=1$ whenever $|S|\le r$, since this suffices to control the observed-data likelihood ratio $\mathrm{d}Q_1/\mathrm{d}Q_0$; see \crtCref{lem:observed-likelihood-ratio-exact}.

label: lem:observed-likelihood-ratio-exact
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:observed-likelihood-ratio-exact}
Recall the definitions of the Boolean hiding function $J(\cdot)$ from \crtCref{eq:def-J}, and the vector $T = (T_1,\ldots,T_m)$ of asymmetric Rademacher random variables from \crtCref{eq:def-T}. 
For every deterministic $U \subseteq [m]$, denote
\[
    J_U(T_U) := \mathbb{E}_0\bigl[J(T) \bigm| T_U\bigr].
\]
The observed-data likelihood ratio based on a single observation $(Y,M,Z)$ satisfies
\[
    \widetilde{L}_\alpha := \frac{\mathrm{d}Q_1}{\mathrm{d}Q_0}(Y,M,Z)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        \displaystyle
        \exp(\alpha V)
        \left\{
            \cosh(\alpha) - V \sinh(\alpha) \cdot J_S(T_S)
        \right\},
        & \text{if}~\, D=1,
        \\
        \displaystyle
        \cosh^2(\alpha) - \sinh^2(\alpha) \cdot J_S(T_S),
        & \text{if}~\, D=0.
    \end{cases}
\]
In particular, $\widetilde{L}_\alpha=1$ on the event $\{|S|\leq r\}$.

label: eq:generic-assouad-alpha-choice
title: Proof
body_md:
Choose
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:generic-assouad-alpha-choice}
    \alpha^2
    :=
    \widetilde{c} \frac{p}{nq\,\mathcal{B}_{m,\lambda,q}},
\end{equation}
where $\widetilde{c}>0$ is a universal constant defined as 
\[
\widetilde{c} := \min\biggl\{\frac{3C}{32},\frac{1}{C} \log(2) \biggr\},
\]
where $C$ is the constant in~\crtCref{eq:generic-assouad-sample-size}.
We first verify that the resulting hypercube satisfies the assumptions of \crtCref{lem:large-R-assouad-validity,lem:large-R-assouad-hamming}. By \crtCref{eq:generic-assouad-sample-size}, we have
\[
    n \ge \frac{C}{\mathcal{B}_{m,\lambda,q}} \frac{p}{q^2}
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    \alpha^2 \le \frac{\widetilde{c}}{C}q \le q,
\]
 
since, by definition, $\widetilde{c} \le 3C/32 < C$. Similarly, since $\|J\|_\infty^2\le G_\lambda^m$ by \crtCref{lem:two-point-validity},
\[
    n \ge \frac{C}{\mathcal{B}_{m,\lambda,q}} \frac{p}{q} \bigl(G_\lambda\bigr)^m
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    \alpha^2\|J\|_\infty^2 \le \frac{\widetilde{c}}{C} \le \frac{1}{4},
\]
since, by definition, $\widetilde{c} \le 3C/32 < C/4$. Thus, $\alpha\|J\|_\infty\le\nicefrac{1}{2}$. Finally,
\[
    n \ge \frac{C}{\mathcal{B}_{m,\lambda,q}} \frac{p^2}{qR^2}
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    p\alpha^2 \le \frac{\widetilde{c}}{C}R^2 \le \frac{3R^2}{32}.
\] 
Therefore, all conditions of \crtCref{lem:large-R-assouad-validity,lem:large-R-assouad-hamming} hold. 
Together with \crtCref{eq:generic-assouad-deterministic-conditions}, \crtCref{lem:large-R-assouad-validity} therefore ensures that every $P_\omega$ belongs to the required model class.
 
Hence, for every $k\in[p]$ and every neighboring pair $\bigl(\omega,\omega^{(k)}\bigr)$, \crtCref{lem:large-R-assouad-hamming} and \crtCref{eq:generic-assouad-alpha-choice} together yield
\[
    \chi^2\left(
        Q_{\omega^{(k)}}^{\otimes n},
        Q_\omega^{\otimes n}
    \right)
    \le
    \exp\left\{
        \frac{Cnq\alpha^2}{p}\,
        \mathcal{B}_{m,\lambda,q}
    \right\}-1
    \overset{\1}{=}
    \exp(\widetilde{c}\,C)-1
    \overset{\2}{\le}
    1,
\]
where step $\1$ follows directly from the definition of $\alpha^2$ in \crtCref{eq:generic-assouad-alpha-choice}, and step $\2$ exploits the fact that $\widetilde{c} \le \frac{1}{C} \log(2)$ which implies $\exp(\widetilde{c}\,C) \le 2$. Lastly, the inequality $d_{\text{TV}}(P,Q) \le \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\chi^2(P,Q)}$ yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:generic-assouad-TV}
    d_{\text{TV}}\left(
        Q_{\omega^{(k)}}^{\otimes n},
        Q_\omega^{\otimes n}
    \right)
    \le
    \frac{1}{2}
\end{equation}
uniformly over all neighboring vertices. 

To complete the proof, we employ a standard Assouad reduction (see, e.g., \citet[Lemma 2.12]{Tsybakov2009}, \citet[Lemma 8.7]{SamworthShah2026modern}). From \crtCref{lem:large-R-assouad-validity}(c), we have separation $8\alpha^2$ in $\ell^2_2$ between two neighboring vertices $\omega$ and $\omega^{(k)}$, and from \crtCref{eq:generic-assouad-TV}, we have that their corresponding observed-data laws are within $1/2$ in total variation distance. Thus, by a calculation similar to the proof of our baseline Assouad minimax risk lower bound in \crtCref{subsec:baseline-assouad}, we obtain
\[
    \mathfrak{R}_n(R,\mu,q)
    \ge
    \frac{p\alpha^2}{2}
    =
    \frac{\widetilde{c}}{2}
    \frac{p^2}
    {nq\,\mathcal{B}_{m,\lambda,q}},
\]
which proves the lemma after renaming $c := \widetilde{c}/2$.

label: claim:phiq-LCM
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{claim:phiq-LCM}
The least concave majorant $\overline\phi_q$ of the function $\phi_q : [0,1] \to [0,\log(1/q)]$ has the closed-form expression given by \crtCref{eq:phiq-LCM-definition}, with the convention that $\overline{\phi}_q(s) = \log(1/q)$ for all $s > 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $q<1$, write
\[
    r_q(s):=\frac{\phi_q(s)}{s}=\frac{\log\bigl(1+\gamma_qs^2\bigr)}{s},\qquad s\in(0,1].
\]
 
Differentiating $r_q(s)$, we obtain
\[
    r_q'(s)
    =
    \frac{1}{s^2}\left\{\frac{2\gamma_qs^2}{1+\gamma_qs^2}-\log\bigl(1+\gamma_qs^2\bigr)\right\}
    =
    \frac{h(\gamma_qs^2)}{s^2},
\]
where we recall from \crtCref{eq:def-h-func} that
\[
    h(x) =\frac{2x}{1+x}-\log(1+x),\qquad\text{for}\,~ x\ge0.
\]
Note that
\[
    h'(x)=\frac{1-x}{(1+x)^2}.
\]
Thus, $h$ is strictly increasing on $[0,1)$ and strictly decreasing on $(1,\infty)$. Since $h(0)=0$, $h(1)=1-\log(2)>0$, and $h(x)\to-\infty$ as $x\to\infty$, there exists a unique $x_\star>1$ such that
$h(x_\star)=0$.


\medskip\noindent
\underline{Case 1 ($q_\star \le q \le 1$)}.
First, consider the case that $q_\star\le q<1$. Then $\gamma_q\le x_\star$, so $h(\gamma_qs^2)\ge0$ for every $s\in[0,1]$. Hence $r_q$ is non-decreasing on $(0,1]$, and therefore
\[
    \phi_q(s)\le s\,\phi_q(1)=s\log\frac{1}{q},\qquad s\in[0,1].
\]
The function $s\mapsto s\log(1/q)$ is a concave majorant of $\phi_q$. Moreover, any concave majorant $g$ of $\phi_q$ satisfies
\[
    g(s) \ge (1-s) \cdot g(0)+s \cdot g(1) \ge s\,\phi_q(1)=s \,\log\frac{1}{q}.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:phi-concave-majorant-large-q}
    \overline\phi_q(s)=s\log\frac{1}{q},\qquad q_\star\le q<1,\quad s\in[0,1].
\end{equation}
For $q=1$, we have $\gamma_q=0$, so $\phi_q\equiv0$, and \crtCref{eq:phi-concave-majorant-large-q} remains valid.

\medskip\noindent
\underline{Case 2 ($0 < q < q_\star$)}.
Now consider the case that $0<q<q_\star$. Then, $\gamma_q>x_\star$. Define
\[
    \tau_q:=\sqrt{\frac{x_\star}{\gamma_q}}=\sqrt{\frac{x_\star q}{1-q}}\in(0,1).
\]

Note that since $r_q'(s) = h(\gamma_qs^2)/s^2$, it has the same sign as $h(\gamma_qs^2)$. Thus, the function $r_q$ is increasing on $(0,\tau_q]$ and decreasing on $[\tau_q,1]$. Hence,
\[
    \phi_q(s)\le\frac{\phi_q(\tau_q)}{\tau_q}s,
    \qquad\text{for}\,~ s\in[0,\tau_q].
\]
Furthermore,
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\phi_q(\tau_q)}{\tau_q}
    &=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_q}{x_\star}}\log(1+x_\star)
    =\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_q}{x_\star}} \frac{2 x_\star}{1+x_\star}
    =2\kappa_\star\sqrt{\gamma_q}.
\end{align*}

 
Also, note that
\[
    \phi_q''(s)=\frac{2\gamma_q(1-\gamma_qs^2)}{(1+\gamma_qs^2)^2}.
\]
Since $x_\star>1$, we have $\tau_q>1/\sqrt{\gamma_q}$, and therefore $\phi_q$ is concave on $[\tau_q,1]$. Moreover,
\[
    \phi_q'(\tau_q)=\frac{2\gamma_q\tau_q}{1+\gamma_q\tau_q^2}=\frac{2\sqrt{\gamma_q x_\star}}{1+x_\star}=2\kappa_\star\sqrt{\gamma_q}=\frac{\phi_q(\tau_q)}{\tau_q}.
\]
Thus, the linear function on $[0,\tau_q]$ joins $\phi_q$ tangentially at $\tau_q$. It follows that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:phi-concave-majorant-small-q}
    \overline\phi_q(s)=
    \begin{cases}
        \displaystyle 2\kappa_\star\sqrt{\tfrac{1-q}{q}}\,s, & 0\le s\le\tau_q,\\ 
        \displaystyle \log\left(1+\tfrac{1-q}{q}s^2\right), & \tau_q\le s\le1.
    \end{cases}
\end{equation}
This proves that $\overline\phi_q$ is a concave majorant of $\phi_q$ on $[0,1]$. To prove minimality, let $g$ be any concave majorant of $\phi_q$. For $s\in[0,\tau_q]$, concavity of $g$ yields
\[
    g(s)
    \ge
    \left(1-\frac{s}{\tau_q}\right)g(0)+\frac{s}{\tau_q}g(\tau_q)
    \ge
    \frac{s}{\tau_q}\phi_q(\tau_q)
    =
    \overline\phi_q(s),
\]
while for $s\in[\tau_q,1]$, we necessarily have $g(s)\ge\phi_q(s)=\overline\phi_q(s)$. Thus, $\overline\phi_q$ is indeed the least concave majorant of $\phi_q$ on $[0,1]$, and given by: 
\begin{equation*}
\overline\phi_q(s)
\,=\,
\begin{cases} 
  \, s\log\frac{1}{q}, &\text{if}\,~ q \in [q_\star,1) ~\text{and}~ s\in[0,1], \\ 
  \, 2\kappa_\star\sqrt{\frac{1-q}{q}}\,s, &\text{if}\,~ q \in (0,q_\star] ~\text{and}~ s\in[0,\tau_q],\\ 
  \, \log\left(1+\frac{1-q}{q}s^2\right), &\text{if}\,~ q \in (0,q_\star] ~\text{and}~ s\in[\tau_q,1].
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
which proves the claim since by convention, we have $\overline{\phi}_q(s) = \log(1/q)$ for $s \geq 1$.

label: claim:xi-D-inc
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{claim:xi-D-inc}
The function $\xi_q : (0,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined in \crtCref{eq:xi-D} is non-decreasing.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Clearly, if $D\le R/2$, then $\xi_q(D)=D\,\overline\phi_q(1)$,
which is non-decreasing in $D$. 
If $D\ge R/2$, denoting $u := R/(2D)\in(0,1]$, we obtain
\[
    \xi_q(D)=\frac{R}{2}\frac{\overline\phi_q(u)}{u}.
\]
 
It thus suffices to show that the map $u\mapsto\overline\phi_q(u)/u$ is non-increasing on $(0,1]$. Take $0 < u < v \leq 1$ and note that by concavity of $\overline\phi_q$ on $[0,1]$ and the fact that $\overline\phi_q(0) = 0$, we have
\begin{align*}
    \overline\phi_q(u) 
    = \overline\phi_q\Bigl( \mfrac{u}{v} \cdot v + \bigl(1 - \mfrac{u}{v}\bigr) \cdot 0 \Bigr)
    \geq \mfrac{u}{v} \cdot \overline\phi_q(v) + \biggl(1 - \mfrac{u}{v}\biggr) \cdot \overline\phi_q(0) 
    = \frac{u}{v} \, \overline\phi_q(v),
\end{align*}
which proves that $\overline\phi_q(u)/u$ is non-increasing in $u$ on $(0,1]$. 
\qed

label: lem:observed-likelihood-ratio-general
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{lem:observed-likelihood-ratio-general}
The distribution $Q_1$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $Q_0$, and
\[
    \frac{\mathrm{d}Q_1}{\mathrm{d}Q_0}(Y,M,Z)
    =
    \mathbb{E}_0 \big[L_\alpha\mid\mathcal{O}\big],
    \qquad
    Q_0\text{-almost surely}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $g=g(Y,M,Z)$ be any bounded and measurable function of the observed data. Since $M$ is independent of $(X,Y)$ and has the same distribution (say, $P_M$) under both hypotheses, the likelihood ratio of the joint law of $(X,Y,M)$ under the alternative with respect to the null is $L_\alpha(X,Y)$. Hence
\begin{align*}
    \int g \, \mathrm{d}Q_1 
    = 
    \mathbb{E}_{Q_1}[g]
    &=
    \int g(y,m,m\odot x)\, P_1(\mathrm dx,\mathrm dy)\, P_M(\mathrm dm)
    \\
    &=
    \int g(y,m,m\odot x)\, L_\alpha(x,y)\, P_0(\mathrm dx,\mathrm dy)\, P_M(\mathrm dm)
    = \mathbb{E}_0\!\bigl[L_\alpha \cdot g(Y,M,Z)\bigr].
\end{align*}
Since $g(Y,M,Z)$ is $\mathcal{O}$-measurable, the tower property yields
\begin{align*}
    \int g \, \mathrm{d}Q_1 
    &=
    \mathbb{E}_0\!\Bigl[
        \mathbb{E}_0\bigl[L_\alpha \cdot g(Y,M,Z) \,\big|\, \mathcal{O}\bigr]
    \Bigr] 
    =
    \mathbb{E}_0 \!\Bigl[
        \mathbb{E}_0\bigl[L_\alpha \big| \mathcal{O}\bigr] \cdot g
    \Bigr] 
    =
    \int \mathbb{E}_0\bigl[L_\alpha \big| \mathcal{O}\bigr] \cdot g \, \mathrm{d}Q_0.
\end{align*}
As this identity holds for every bounded and measurable $g$, it follows that $Q_1\ll Q_0$ and
\[
    \frac{\mathrm{d}Q_1}{\mathrm{d}Q_0}(Y,M,Z)
    =
    \mathbb{E}_0 \bigl[L_\alpha\mid\mathcal{O}\bigr],
\]
$Q_0$-almost surely, as desired. \hfill \qed

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:V-independence}
Recall the definition of $V$ from \crtCref{eq:def-V}. Under $P_0$, $V$ is a uniform Rademacher random variable independent of ~$(Y,T_1,\ldots,T_m)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: manual
name: part (a

title: Proof
body_md:
The almost sure bound on $\| X \|$ holds by construction, so we focus on lower bounding $\mathbb{E}_{\omega}[X X^{\top}]$.

Conditional on $K=k$, the distribution of $(A,B,Y)$ is either $P_0$ or $P_1$, depending on whether $\omega_k=0$ or $\omega_k=1$. Since $m\ge5$, \crtCref{lem:two-point-validity}(c) shows that the second-moment matrix of $(A,B)$ is the same under these two distributions.
Consequently, conditional on $K=k$,
\[
    \mathbb{E}_\omega[A_j A_{\ell}\mid K=k]
    =
    \mathbb{E}_0[A_j A_{\ell}],
    \qquad
    \mathbb{E}_\omega[A_j B\mid K=k]=0,
    \qquad
    \mathbb{E}_\omega[B^2 \mid K=k]=1,
\]
independently of the value of $\omega_k$.

Averaging over the uniform random variable $K$, we therefore obtain
\[
    \mathbb{E}_\omega[XX^\top]
    =
    \frac{1}{2}
    \begin{bmatrix}
        \mfrac{1}{m}
        \left\{
            (1-\rho^2)I_m
            +
            \rho^2\boldsymbol 1_m\boldsymbol 1_m^\top
        \right\} & 0 \\ 
        0 & \mfrac{1}{p} I_p
    \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The smallest eigenvalues of the upper-left and lower-right blocks are $\frac{1-\rho^2}{2m}$ and $1/(2p)$, respectively. Hence, for all $\omega \in \{0,1\}^p$,
\[
    \mathbb{E}_\omega[XX^\top]
    \succeq
    \frac{1}{2}
    \min\left\{
        \frac{1-\rho^2}{m},
        \frac{1}{p}
    \right\}
    I_{m+p}.
\]

label: lem:majority-coefficients

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first consider the case in which $\lvert U \rvert$ is even.  Recall that
\[
g_U = \frac{1}{2^m} \sum_{t\in\{-1,1\}^m} f(t) \, \chi_U(t).
\]
Since the majority function is odd and the Fourier characters satisfy $\chi_U(-x)=(-1)^{|U|}\chi_U(x)$, it follows that $g_U = (-1)^{|U|+1}g_U$.  Since $\lvert U \rvert$ is even, we deduce that $g_U = 0$. 

Next, consider the case in which $\lvert U \rvert$ is  odd.  For $x\in\{-1,1\}^m$, define the set $C(x) \subseteq [m]$ to denote the indices of the negative components of $x$:
\[
    C(x):=\{j\in[m]:x_j=-1\},
\]
and use this to write the Fourier characters as $\chi_U(x)=(-1)^{|C(x)\cap U|}$.  Further, note that since $m = 2r + 1$, it holds that $f(x) = 1$ if and only if $\lvert C(x) \rvert \leq r$.  Combining these two facts yields the equivalent representation 
\[
g_U 
= \frac{1}{2^m} \sum_{t\in\{-1,1\}^m} f(t) \, \chi_U(t) 
= \frac{1}{2^m} \sum_{C \subseteq [m]} f_C \cdot (-1)^{|C\cap U|},
\]
where $f_C=1$ if $|C|\leq r$, and $f_C=-1$ if $|C|\geq r+1$.

Continuing, pair every set $C\subseteq[m]$ with its complement $C^c$. Since $m=2r+1$, exactly one member of each pair has cardinality at most $r$. Moreover, $f_{C^c}=-f_C$, and
\[
    (-1)^{|C^c\cap U|}
    =
    (-1)^{|U|-|C\cap U|}
    =
    -(-1)^{|C\cap U|},
\]
where the last equality uses the fact that $|U|$ is odd. Hence the two terms in each pair are equal. It thus follows that
\[
    g_U
    =
    \frac{1}{2^{m-1}}
    \sum_{\substack{C\subseteq[m]\\|C|\leq r}}
    (-1)^{|C\cap U|},
\]
as desired.

Finally, we note that the relation $\sum_{U \subseteq [m]} g_U^2 = 1$ follows from Parseval's identity.

label: lem:boolean-cancellation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:boolean-cancellation}
Let $r \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$ and let $m = 2r + 1$.  The Fourier coefficients $\{g_U\}_{U \subseteq [m]}$ of the majority function satisfy the following.  For every $S\subseteq[m]$ satisfying $|S|\leq r$, and every $C\subseteq S$,
\[
    \sum_{\substack{
        U \subseteq [m],\\
        |U|\ \mathrm{odd},\\
        U\cap S=C
    }} g_U
    \,=\,
    \mathbbm{1}\{C=\varnothing\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $S\subseteq[m]$ with $|S|\leq r$. For every $x_S\in\{-1,1\}^S$, consider the vector $(x_S,\boldsymbol{1}_{S^c})\in\{-1,1\}^m$. Regardless of the values of $x_S$, this vector has at least $m-|S|$ positive coordinates and at most $|S|$ negative coordinates. Since
\[
    m-|S| \geq 2r+1-r = r+1 > |S|,
\]
the positive coordinates form a strict majority. Therefore,
\[
    f(x_S,\boldsymbol{1}_{S^c})=1
    \qquad
    \text{for every}\,~x_S\in\{-1,1\}^S.
\]
 
Using the Fourier expansion of $f$, we thus have
\begin{align}
    1
    =
    f(x_S,\boldsymbol{1}_{S^c})
    =
    \sum_{U\subseteq[m]} g_U \chi_U(x_S,\boldsymbol{1}_{S^c}) \nonumber
    &=
    \sum_{U\subseteq[m]} g_U \prod_{j\in U\cap S} x_j \nonumber \\
    &=
    \sum_{C\subseteq S} \Bigg(\sum_{\substack{U\subseteq[m]\\U\cap S=C}} g_U\Bigg) \prod_{j\in C} x_j \nonumber\\
    &=
    \Bigg(\sum_{\substack{U\subseteq[m]\\U\cap S=\varnothing}} g_U\Bigg) +
    \sum_{\varnothing \neq C\subseteq S} \Bigg(\sum_{\substack{U\subseteq[m]\\U\cap S=C}} g_U\Bigg) \prod_{j\in C} x_j.
\label{eq:extended-maj-fourier-1}
\end{align}

On the other hand, note that the constant function $1$ has Fourier coefficient $1$ at $C=\varnothing$ and $0$ otherwise, since
\begin{align}
\label{eq:extended-maj-fourier-2}
    1
    =
    1 + \sum_{\varnothing \neq C\subseteq S} 0 \cdot \prod_{j\in C} x_j
\end{align}

Since the functions $\{\chi_C:C\subseteq S\}$ form an orthonormal basis for the space of real-valued functions on $\{-1,1\}^S$~\citep[Theorem~1.5]{odonnell2021analysisbooleanfunctions}, the Fourier expansion is unique. Therefore, comparing the Fourier coefficients of $f(x_S,\boldsymbol{1}_{S^c}) \equiv 1$ from \crtCref{eq:extended-maj-fourier-1,eq:extended-maj-fourier-2}, we obtain
\[
    \sum_{\substack{U\subseteq[m]\\U\cap S=C}} g_U
    =
    \mathbbm{1}\{C=\varnothing\},
    \qquad\text{for every}\,~ C\subseteq S.
\]

Finally, we use the result from \crtCref{lem:majority-coefficients}~\citep[or,][Theorem~5.19]{odonnell2021analysisbooleanfunctions} that $g_U=0$ for every even-cardinality $U$, so the inner sum may equivalently be restricted to odd-cardinality $U$. Thus,
\[
    \sum_{\substack{
        U \subseteq [m]\\
        |U|\ \mathrm{odd}\\
        U\cap S=C
    }}
    g_U
    \,=\,
    \mathbbm{1}\{C = \varnothing\},
\]
which completes the proof.

label: lem:exact-hU
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:exact-hU}
For each $U \subseteq [m]$, the quantity $h_U$ as in \crtCref{eq:def-hU} depends only on $k:=|U|$, and has the following closed-form expression
\[
    h_U
    =
    \begin{cases}
        \, 1, & \text{if}\;~ k=0, \\ 
        \, 0, & \text{if}\;~ 1\le k\le r, \\ 
        \, \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{2^{k-1}} \, (-1)^r \, \binom{k-1}{r}, & \text{if}\;~ r+1\le k\le m.
    \end{cases}
\]
head: environment

label: eq:hU-restricted-Fourier
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $U \subseteq [m]$, and write $k:=|U|$. Define the restriction
\[
    f_U(z) := f(z,\boldsymbol 1_{U^c}),
    \qquad
    \text{for}\;~z\in\{-1,1\}^U.
\]
Restricting the Fourier expansion of $f$ gives
\[
    f_U(z) = \sum_{W\subseteq[m]}g_W \cdot \chi_{W\cap U}(z).
\]
Therefore, the Fourier coefficient of the full monomial $\chi_U$ in $f_U$ is
\[
    \widehat{f}_U(U) = \sum_{W\supseteq U}g_W = h_U.
\]
Hence,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hU-restricted-Fourier}
    h_U
    =
    \frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{z\in\{-1,1\}^U} f_U(z) \cdot \chi_U(z).
\end{equation}

Suppose that $z$ has exactly $j$ coordinates equal to $-1$. Then, $\chi_U(z)=(-1)^j$, and the sum of all $m$ coordinates of $(z,\boldsymbol 1_{U^c})$ is
\[
    (m-k)+(k-2j) = m-2j = 2(r-j)+1.
\]
Since $m=2r+1$,
\[
    f_U(z)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        +1, & \text{if}\,~ j\le r,\\
        -1, & \text{if}\,~ j\ge r+1.
    \end{cases}
\]
Thus,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hU-binomial-sum}
    h_U
    = 2^{-k}
    \left\{
        \sum_{j=0}^{\min\{r,k\}}
        (-1)^j\binom{k}{j}
        -
        \sum_{j=r+1}^{k}
        (-1)^j\binom{k}{j}
    \right\},
\end{equation}
where the second sum is $0$ when $k\le r$.

\begin{itemize}
\item 
If $k=0$, then $h_\varnothing=f(\boldsymbol 1_m)=1$. Suppose henceforth that $k\ge1$. Since
\[
    \sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^j\binom{k}{j}=0,
\]
\crtCref{eq:hU-binomial-sum} becomes
\[
    h_U
    =
    2^{1-k} \sum_{j=0}^{\min\{r,k\}} (-1)^j\binom{k}{j}.
\]
\item 
If $1\le k\le r$, the sum on the right is the complete alternating binomial sum, and hence $h_U=0$.

\item
If $k\ge r+1$,  we have
\begin{align*}
    h_U = 2^{1-k} \sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^j\binom{k}{j}
    &=
    2^{1-k} \sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^j
    \left\{
        \binom{k-1}{j}
        +
        \binom{k-1}{j-1}
    \right\}
    \\
    &=
    2^{1-k} \left[\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^j\binom{k-1}{j}
    -
    \sum_{j=0}^{r-1}(-1)^j\binom{k-1}{j}\right]
    \\
    &=
    \frac{1}{2^{k-1}} (-1)^r\binom{k-1}{r}.
\end{align*}
\end{itemize}
This proves the claimed formula.

label: lem:two-dimensional-patch
title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
When $m=1$, the majority function is $f(t)=t$, so $g_{\{1\}}=1$ and hence $J(T)=\frac{T}{\rho}$.

The null covariance follows from $X=(A,B)^\top/\sqrt2$, together with
$A^2=B^2=1$ and $\mathbb{E}_0[AB]=0$. Under the alternative,
$AB=TV$ and
\[
    L_\alpha
    =
    e^{\alpha V}
    \left\{
        \cosh(\alpha) - V\sinh(\alpha) \cdot \frac{T}{\rho}
    \right\}.
\]
Since $T\perp\hspace{-2.3mm}\perp V$ under $P_0$, $\mathbb{E}_0[T]=\rho$, $T^2=1$, and
\[
    \mathbb{E}_0[e^{\alpha V}]=\cosh(\alpha),
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \mathbb{E}_0[Ve^{\alpha V}]=\sinh(\alpha),
\]
we obtain
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}_1[AB]
    =\mathbb{E}_0[L_\alpha TV]
    &=
    \cosh(\alpha) \cdot \mathbb{E}_0[T] \cdot \mathbb{E}_0[Ve^{\alpha V}]
    -
    \frac{\sinh(\alpha)}{\rho} \cdot \mathbb{E}_0[T^2] \cdot \mathbb{E}_0[e^{\alpha V}] \\
    &=
    \cosh(\alpha)\sinh(\alpha)
    \left(\rho-\frac{1}{\rho}\right) \\
    &=
    \frac{1}{2}\sinh(2\alpha) \cdot 
    \left(\tanh(\lambda)-\coth(\lambda)\right) \\ 
    &=
    -\frac{1}{2}\sinh(2\alpha) \cdot \frac{2}{\sinh(2\lambda)} 
    =
    -\frac{\sinh(2\alpha)}{\sinh(2\lambda)}.
\end{align*}
Since $A^2=B^2=1$, the diagonal entries remain equal to $1/2$, and hence
\[
    \mathbb{E}_1[XX^\top]
    =
    \frac{1}{2}
    \begin{bmatrix}
        1 & -\mfrac{\sinh(2\alpha)}{\sinh(2\lambda)} \\ 
        -\mfrac{\sinh(2\alpha)}{\sinh(2\lambda)} & 1
    \end{bmatrix}
    \succeq
    \frac{1}{2}\left\{1-\frac{\sinh(2\alpha)}{\sinh(2\lambda)}\right\} I_2.
\]

The conditions $\alpha\le\rho/2$ and $8(\lambda^2+\alpha^2)\le R^2$ ensure, respectively, that $\alpha\|J\|_\infty\le1/2$ and that both parameters belong to $\Theta_R$. The assumption
\[
    \frac{\sinh(2\alpha)}{\sinh(2\lambda)}\le1-2\mu
\]
yields $\mathbb{E}_1[XX^\top]\succeq\mu I_2$, while $\mathbb{E}_0[XX^\top]=I_2/2\succeq\mu I_2$.

Also, since \(J(T)=T/\rho\), a direct calculation gives
\[
\mathcal{W}_{1,q}
= q\,\mathbb{E}_0\left[\left(\frac{T}{\rho}-1\right)^2\right]
= \frac{q(1-\rho^2)}{\rho^2}
= \frac{q}{\sinh^2(\lambda)}.
\]

Finally, note that whenever $0 < \alpha^2 \le q$, \crtCref{eq:exact-observed-chi-square} and \crtCref{lem:two-point-divergence} jointly imply that there exists a sufficiently large universal constant $C' > 0$ such that
\[
    \chi^2(Q_1,Q_0)
    \le C q\alpha^2\mathcal{W}_{1,q}
    = C'\frac{q^2\alpha^2}{\sinh^2(\lambda)}.
\]
Thus, with $\alpha^2=\frac{c'}{C'} \frac{\sinh^2(\lambda)}{nq^2}$, tensorization yields
\[
    \chi^2\left(Q_1^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n}\right)\le\exp(c')-1.
\]
Choosing $c'>0$ sufficiently small makes the corresponding total variation distance at most $1/2$. Since $\|\theta_1-\theta_0\|_2^2=8\alpha^2$, a standard application of Le Cam's two-point inequality (see, e.g., \citet{Wainwright2019highdim,SamworthShah2026modern}) gives the claimed lower bound.

label: lem:moderate-mu-lower-bound
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $h:=\min\{R\mu,1\}$. Set
\[
    \lambda:=\frac{h}{8},
    \quad~\text{and}\quad~
    \alpha^2:=c'' \frac{\sinh^2(\lambda)}{nq^2}.
\]
Since $R\mu>\sqrt{q}$, we have $\sqrt{q}\le h\le1$ and $0<\lambda\le1/8$. Also, the sample-size condition $n \ge Cq^{-3}$ implies that $1/(nq^2)\le q/C\le1/C$. In particular,
\[
    \alpha^2\le\frac{c'' \sinh^2(1/8)}{C}\,q\le q,
    \quad\;\text{and}\quad\;
    \frac{\alpha}{\tanh(\lambda)}
    =\cosh(\lambda)\sqrt{\frac{c''}{nq^2}}
    \le\cosh(1/8)\sqrt{\frac{c''}{C}}\le\frac{1}{2},
\]
after increasing $C$ if necessary.

We next verify the curvature condition. Since $\alpha^2\le q\le1$, we have $\alpha\le1$. Therefore, using $\sinh(2\alpha)\le2\alpha\cosh(2\alpha)\le2\alpha\cosh(2)$ and $\sinh(2\lambda)\ge2\lambda$,
\[
    \frac{\sinh(2\alpha)}{\sinh(2\lambda)}
    \le
    \cosh(2) \cdot \frac{\alpha}{\lambda}
    \le
    C\sqrt{\frac{c''}{nq^2}}
    \le
    C\sqrt{\frac{c''}{C}}
    \le\frac{1}{3} \le 1-2\mu,
\]
for $C$ sufficiently large. Finally, $h\le R\mu$ and $\mu\le1/3$ give $8\lambda^2=h^2/8\le R^2/72$. Moreover,
\[
    \alpha^2
    \le
    \frac{c''\cosh^2(1/8)}{64C}\,h^2,
\]
so, after increasing $C$ once more, $8(\lambda^2+\alpha^2)\le R^2$. Thus all the conditions of \crtCref{lem:two-dimensional-patch} are satisfied.
 
Since $\sinh(\lambda)\ge\lambda=h/8$, \crtCref{eq:two-dimensional-patch-lower} yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:moderate-mu-two-dimensional-bound}
    \mathfrak{R}_n(R,\mu,q)
    \ge
    c\frac{h^2}{nq^2}.
\end{equation}

We also use the baseline lower bound from \crtCref{prop:baseline-assouad}. Since $R\mu>\sqrt{q}$, we have $R^2>q/\mu^2$, and therefore
\[
    \frac{1}{q\mu^2R^2}<\frac{1}{q^2}.
\]
Thus, under the minimum sample size assumption $n\ge C q^{-3}$, we have $1/(nq\mu^2)\le R^2$. Since $\exp(R/4)\ge1$, \crtCref{prop:baseline-assouad} consequently yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:moderate-mu-baseline-bound}
    \mathfrak{R}_n(R,\mu,q)\ge\frac{c}{nq\mu^2}.
\end{equation}

Finally, choose a sufficiently small universal constant $c_1\in(0,\mu_{\mathrm{crit}})$, and define $\eta:=c_1/\mu\in(0,1)$ and $y:=(1-q)h^2/q$. Since $s\mapsto s^\eta$ is concave on $[0,\infty)$,
\[
    \frac{1}{nq\mu^2}(1+y)^\eta
    \le
    \frac{1}{nq\mu^2}(1+y)
    \le
    \frac{1}{nq\mu^2}
    +
    \frac{h^2}{nq^2\mu_{\mathrm{crit}}^2}.
\]
Combining \crtCref{eq:moderate-mu-two-dimensional-bound,eq:moderate-mu-baseline-bound}, and adjusting the universal constant gives
\begin{equation*}
    \mathfrak{R}_n(R,\mu,q)
    \ge
    \frac{c_0}{nq\mu^2}
    \exp\biggl\{
        \frac{c_1}{\mu}
        \log\biggl(
            1+\frac{1-q}{q}\min\{R^2\mu^2,1\}
        \biggr)
    \biggr\},
\end{equation*}
where we used $h^2=\min\{R^2\mu^2,1\}$. This completes the proof.
